Cardiology and hematology · published research

Vasoconstriction

One microswine experiment found acute widening of arteries after local laser delivery to histamine-induced spasm. No clinical study has tested this effect in people.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Red and near-infrared laser exposure produced acute relaxation of histamine-induced arterial spasm in a small atherosclerotic microswine experiment. The effect was observed during angiographic follow-up, but clinical relevance, durability, and human treatment effects remain unknown.

Human and clinical evidence

No human intervention study was identified. The experiment did not involve people with coronary vasospasm, Raynaud syndrome, or another clinical vasoconstrictive disorder.

Animal evidence

Histamine-induced narrowing was produced in 13 arteries from ten atherosclerotic Yucatan microswine. Visible red 632 nm light completely reversed spasm in two of four treated arteries and reduced narrowing in the remaining two. Near-infrared 1,064 nm light reduced narrowing in all three treated arteries. The mean increase in luminal diameter was greater than during the corresponding control trials, while three sham fiber-optic trials did not produce comparable relaxation (Gal et al. 1992).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment compared ultraviolet 351 nm, visible red 632 nm, and near-infrared 1,064 nm light delivered percutaneously through fiber optics to the site of spasm. Ultraviolet exposure is outside the usual red and near-infrared PBM range and should not be treated as an equivalent PBM protocol. Angiography followed the acute response for up to 30 minutes. The publication does not establish a human dose, delivery route, or treatment schedule.

Interpretation

The study demonstrates acute photorelaxation of experimentally constricted arteries under the tested conditions. Because it is a single small animal experiment using local fiber-optic delivery, it does not establish durable vasodilation or clinical treatment benefit.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for reversing arterial spasm in people. Evidence is limited to one small animal experiment and does not establish a durable or clinically usable treatment.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Certainty is very low because the evidence comes from one small microswine experiment with histamine-induced arterial spasm. Each wavelength was tested in only three or four arteries, there was no independent replication or human treatment study, and the catheter-based delivery model does not establish a clinically usable protocol or durable benefit (Gal et al. 1992).
